title: Do sin taxes work?
summary: Josh and Chuck examine "sin taxes" on products like soda, tobacco, and alcohol, asking whether they actually work. They cover Mayor Bloomberg's failed New York soda ban and the later Berkeley soda tax, the San Francisco spillover question, Mexico's soda and junk food taxes, and the history of excise taxes from the whiskey tax and the Whiskey Rebellion to sumptuary laws and the 1764 sugar tax. They discuss Illinois alcohol tax and drunk driving data, the Canadian and Arkansas cigarette tax backfires (black markets and lost revenue), and whether sin taxes are regressive. The episode concludes with a listener email about logical fallacies and a closing anecdote.

segments.title: Opening banter and Bloomberg's soda ban
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open by referencing an earlier episode on fat taxes and Mayor Bloomberg's failed attempt to ban large sugary sodas in New York City, which a court struck down. They note the article's one-sided framing of sin taxes and introduce the basic definition of a sin tax.

segments.title: What sin taxes are and the case for them
segments.summary: The hosts define sin taxes as excise taxes on goods society views as harmful, such as tobacco, alcohol, and gambling. They explain two justifications: discouraging use, and offsetting social costs like healthcare. They discuss earmarked revenue and public trust in government spending.

segments.title: Berkeley soda tax and San Francisco spillover
segments.summary: Bloomberg's foundation backed a shift to taxes after the ban failed. Berkeley passed a soda tax of about a penny per ounce despite industry spending. A study found consumption fell among low-income and minority Berkeley residents but rose about four percent in nearby San Francisco over five months.

segments.title: Mexico soda and junk food taxes and the diet versus exercise debate
segments.summary: Mexico adopted a soda tax and an eight percent junk food tax, partly after Bloomberg-funded campaigning and concerns about obesity. Consumption of both fell. The soda industry argued exercise matters more, while the hosts note diet is considered more responsible for obesity.

segments.title: History of taxes on vice: whiskey tax, sumptuary laws, and the 1764 sugar tax
segments.summary: Hosts recall that excise taxes on alcohol and tobacco once supplied most US federal revenue, and that the first domestic federal tax was the whiskey tax leading to the Whiskey Rebellion. They describe sumptuary laws under Elizabeth I and George Mason's proposal at the Constitutional Convention, which was rejected in favor of taxes. They mention the 1764 sugar tax.

segments.title: Alcohol taxes, drunk driving, and the sweet spot debate
segments.summary: Illinois raised alcohol taxes in 2009, and drunk driving deaths fell. Mathematics professor Rebecca Golden argued the drop was correlation and linked it to the Great Recession. Hosts discuss that tax increases must be large enough to matter but not so high they backfire, describing a window where taxes work.

segments.title: Cigarette tax backfires: Canada, Arkansas, and black markets
segments.summary: Canada's high cigarette taxes in the early nineties fueled a black market, with black market share rising sharply within five years and government revenue falling. Arkansas doubled its cigarette tax in 2009 and collected about ten million dollars less than the prior year, as buyers crossed state lines.

segments.title: Regressive versus progressive sin taxes and US revenue
segments.summary: Sin taxes are excise taxes that hit poorer people harder as a share of income, though some argue they are progressive because poorer people smoke more and are thus discouraged. The hosts cite US sin tax revenue of about ninety billion dollars and note that governments depend on it. They mention the Adam Smith Institute critique and UK minimum alcohol pricing debate.

segments.title: Wrap-up, listener email, and sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh say they are ambivalent about sin taxes and mention natural experiments in Navajo Nation and elsewhere. They read a listener email from Ada about logical fallacies (straw man and ad hominem) in an earlier hunting episode, followed by a sign-off with contact information. Off-topic talk covers Bloody Mary recipes and Michelada drinks.
